project_name: BioValue AI demo: fictional softwood kraft lignin stream
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.
1 piece(s) of input or evidence text read like instructions to the AI and were replaced before the agents saw them (see the execution trace).

constraints: The stream is currently routed to internal fuel use, so diversion to a sale pathway would require changing that use.
The mill has no lignin dryer, so buyers requiring dry powder would need to provide or install drying capacity.
The mill has no solvent or membrane fractionation equipment, limiting pathways that require fractionated lignin.
The mill has no chemical-modification equipment, limiting pathways that require modified lignin.
The lignin leaves the mill as wet cake, so moisture increases shipping mass and affects downstream handling.
Missing molecular-weight, phenolic-hydroxyl, and sodium data prevent checking requirements that depend on those properties.
data_quality_notes: The record is explicitly fictional demo data and is not representative of measurements from a real mill.
All recorded quantities, composition values, ranges, infrastructure details, and logistics assumptions must be replaced or verified with mill records and laboratory data before decisions are made.
The lignin-content analytical method is unclear for comparison with buyer specifications.
Moisture is identified as uncertain and should be logged over time.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are missing.
The dry-matter balance and composition-total checks passed, and no validation inconsistencies were reported.
agent.summary: Validated fictional softwood kraft lignin filter-cake profile: the recorded wet quantity and moisture convert to the reported canonical wet mass, moisture fraction, and dry mass, with no failed validation checks but several material data gaps.

data_gaps.next_step: Replace the profile with the mill's own lab data and production records.

data_gaps.impact: Molecular weight can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.

data_gaps.impact: Phenolic hydroxyl content can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.

data_gaps.impact: The make-up of the ash is unknown, so ash-related requirements can only be checked against total ash.
data_gaps.next_step: Request an inorganic element analysis of the ash.

data_gaps.impact: Reported lignin content depends on what the analysis counts. The method here is stated for illustration only.
data_gaps.next_step: Confirm the analytical method with the lab and use the same one when comparing with buyers' specifications.

data_gaps.impact: Moisture sets the dry tonnage (dry matter = wet quantity x (1 - moisture)) and the mass that has to be shipped.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#1: UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#3: UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#3: A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can be used as a partial phenol replacement in phenol-formaldehyde resins for adhesives serving plywood and other wood-based panels.
Lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin is reported for veneer plywood and can meet EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 according to vendor technical literature.

target_customers.statement: Potential customer types include plywood producers and manufacturers of wood-based panels that use phenol-formaldehyde adhesives.

competing_materials.statement: The primary incumbent material is phenol used in phenol-formaldehyde resins.

qualification_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin requires an activation or depolymerization step before use in phenol-formaldehyde resins.
One reported process used depolymerized lignin with molecular weight of 800-1,700 g/mol, although the evidence notes this describes process lignin rather than a general delivered-lignin requirement.
Reported plywood qualification includes EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 and formaldehyde testing under EN 717-2.

limitations: The evidence combines reviews, vendor literature, a techno-economic comparison, and a laboratory plywood study.
The strongest commercial-performance evidence is a vendor claim, and the source does not provide an independent test report.
The reported TRL 8 applies to biobased phenolic resins generally rather than specifically to kraft lignin.
Replacement levels and the reported cost estimate are not evidence of demand for this particular fictional mill stream.
missing_information: No named buyers, purchase contracts, regional demand, current lignin price, or expected sales volume is provided.
No delivered wet-cake moisture specification, drying requirement, or logistics acceptance criteria is provided.
The evidence does not establish whether this stream meets the relevant molecular-weight, ash, or activation requirements.

market_evidence.rationale: The pathway has evidence of industrially proven LPF resin from a lignin producer and documented plywood qualification, which supports the rubric's commercial-sales level, although the evidence is concentrated in vendor literature and does not identify buyers.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#1: Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#1: The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
supported_claims.EV-PU-05#1: Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin has been studied as a partial replacement for petroleum-based polyols in rigid polyurethane and polyisocyanurate foams.
Unmodified kraft lignin has also been tested as a replacement for petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam, where the study suggests denser, stiffer foam may suit heavy-duty applications.

target_customers.statement: Potential customer types include rigid insulation-foam producers and manufacturers of flexible or heavy-duty polyurethane foam.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material is petroleum-based polyol used in polyurethane formulations.

qualification_requirements.statement: A cited acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production is total hydroxyl value above 200 mg KOH/g, equivalent to 3.56 mmol/g total hydroxyl groups; this is not a phenolic-hydroxyl requirement.
Kraft lignin generally needs significant treatment, such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction, to reach target polyurethane properties.
Rigid foam qualification in one study used ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.

limitations: Most evidence is from laboratory foam studies, and the published studies report mixed performance for kraft lignin.
The cited TRL 6 applies to a broad polyurethane row including foams, panels, coatings, and rubber replacement, not specifically to kraft-lignin foam.
Commercialization remains limited by consistency, technical performance, and production cost according to an abstract-only review.
Some evidence concerns hardwood kraft lignin, while the project describes a fictional softwood kraft stream.
missing_information: No named polyurethane buyers, commercial sales, contracts, regional demand, current polyol or lignin prices, or expected sales volume is provided.
The evidence does not establish whether the fictional stream meets total hydroxyl, viscosity, solubility, odor, or moisture requirements.
No evidence identifies a commercial formulation partner or validates performance at industrial production scale.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence shows research testing and a broader TRL assessment, but it does not document commercial sales, established buyers, or a market qualification partnership for kraft-lignin polyurethane products.

supported_claims.EV-CM-01#1: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#3: Softwood lignin gives high carbon yields (55% or more) but is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent; hardwood lignin is the reverse, with slightly lower yield (50-55%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#4: Mechanical properties of lignin-based carbon fibers were about 50% of the target in this work.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#1: DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#2: The precursor accounts for about 50% of carbon fiber manufacturing cost.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#2: The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#R1: Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#3: Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.

applications.statement: Lignin can be used as a precursor for carbon fiber, although the evidence reports purification, melt-spinning, and mechanical-performance challenges.

Kraft lignin can be converted into hard carbon for sodium-ion battery anodes, and kraft-lignin hard carbon carbonized at 1,200 °C showed higher initial coulombic efficiency than hard carbon from sulfonated lignin in the cited comparison.
Lignin can be converted into activated carbon, including when the precursor is too impure for other carbon-material applications.

target_customers.statement: Potential customer types include carbon-fiber manufacturers and users of carbon fiber for automotive applications.
Potential customer types include sodium-ion battery-material manufacturers and battery manufacturers or carmakers involved in anode-material qualification.
Potential customer types include activated-carbon producers.

competing_materials.statement: PAN-based carbon fiber is an incumbent or competing material for carbon fiber.
Anthracite and cellulose are feedstock comparators for sodium-ion battery hard carbon; the evidence also identifies fossil precursors such as anthracite or pitch as competing materials.
Conventional activated carbon is the relevant competing product category for lignin-derived activated carbon.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited ORNL carbon-fiber precursor specification requires lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, volatile material below 5% at 250 °C, and removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
Kraft lignin examined for carbon fiber needed purification, and softwood lignin needed a plasticizing or alloying agent for melt spinning.
Activated carbon has no strict precursor-quality limitation, but lower ash improves yield and carbon conversion.
Qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years according to the cited company material.

limitations: The carbon-material pathway combines three products with substantially different requirements; carbon-fiber specifications should not be applied to hard carbon or activated carbon.
Carbon-fiber evidence includes older 2009 work, secondhand specifications, and a modelled rather than measured cost estimate.
The GreenLight and Lignode evidence includes project or company claims; the Lignode plans were reported as of 2021 and later status was not verified.
Hard-carbon evidence is a review, and activated-carbon evidence is laboratory work using zinc chloride activation.
missing_information: No named carbon-fiber, hard-carbon, or activated-carbon purchase customers, contracts, regional demand, or expected sales volume is provided.
No delivered-lignin price, product price, conversion yield for this stream, or route-specific operating cost is provided.
The evidence does not establish whether the fictional stream meets carbon-fiber purity, ash, volatile, carbohydrate, particulate, or battery-grade specifications.
No qualification requirement is provided for activated-carbon customer performance metrics such as adsorption capacity.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents an industrially relevant precursor-fiber project, a pilot production line and qualification activity for lignin-based battery anode material, and therefore goes beyond research-only interest; however, it does not document several producers selling to established buyers.

processing_requirements.statement: The kraft lignin would require activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resins.
The mill would need to address wet-cake handling and likely buyer-side or new mill drying because the stream is wet cake and the mill has no lignin dryer.
Product qualification would require demonstrating the reported plywood bonding and formaldehyde performance requirements.

technical_maturity.statement: Biobased phenolic-resin production is reported at TRL 8.

adoption_barriers.statement: Phenol is the primary incumbent, so resin customers would need to qualify lignin-containing formulations against an established petroleum-derived input.
Potential customers are plywood and wood-based-panel producers, but no named buyers, contracts, regional demand, or expected sales volume has been identified.
The stream's molecular-weight, ash, and activation status are not established, and missing molecular-weight data prevents checking requirements that depend on that property.

assumptions: The economics used fictional wet feedstock mass of 36000.0 / 40000.0 / 43000.0 t/yr across the conservative, base, and optimistic cases.
The economics used fictional moisture of 40.0 / 35.0 / 30.0% of wet mass across the conservative, base, and optimistic cases.
The economics used fictional availability fractions of 40.0 / 50.0 / 60.0% across the conservative, base, and optimistic cases.
The economics calculated dry mass and usable dry feedstock but did not assume a product yield, product price, or variable cost.
Diversion from internal fuel use is assumed to be operationally possible, although it requires changing the current use.
uncertainties: Product output, revenue, variable cost, gross contribution, contribution per tonne, and the indicative-economics score could not be calculated because product yield, product price, and variable costs are missing.
Feedstock compatibility was not scored because the evidence library supplied no numeric requirements for this pathway.

Commercialization feasibility is judged as requiring major additions or a partner: activation or depolymerization, drying arrangements, customer qualification, and buyer development are not currently established.
The cited TRL concerns the technology generally and does not establish that this fictional wet-cake stream meets customer specifications.

commercialization_feasibility.rationale: This pathway has relatively mature supporting technology, but the mill lacks a dryer and the route requires activation or depolymerization before qualification; buyers and contracts are also not identified. It therefore needs major new processing capability and commercial partners rather than being launchable with existing assets.

documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
Softwood lignin gives high carbon yields (55% or more) but is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent; hardwood lignin is the reverse, with slightly lower yield (50-55%).
Mechanical properties of lignin-based carbon fibers were about 50% of the target in this work.
Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
The precursor accounts for about 50% of carbon fiber manufacturing cost.
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.

The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
